{{Short description|Model used to describe wear}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2019|cs1-dates=y}}
{{Use list-defined references|date=January 2022}}
The '''Archard wear equation''' is a simple [[mathematical model|model]] used to describe sliding [[wear]] and is based on the theory of [[Asperity (materials science)|asperity]] contact. The Archard equation was developed much later than '''{{Interlanguage link|Reye's hypothesis|it|Ipotesi di Reye}}''' (sometimes also known as '''energy dissipative hypothesis'''), though both came to the [[multiple discovery|same physical conclusions]], that the volume of the removed debris due to [[wear]] is proportional to the work done by friction forces. [[Theodor Reye]]'s model<ref name="Reye_1860"/><ref name="Rühlmann_1979"/> became popular in Europe and it is still taught in university courses of [[applied mechanics]].<ref name="Villaggio_2001"/> Until recently, Reye's theory of 1860 has, however, been totally ignored in English and American literature<ref name="Villaggio_2001"/> where subsequent works by [[Ragnar Holm]]<ref name="Holm_1946"/><ref name="Holm_1958"/><ref name="Holm_1967"/> and [[John Frederick Archard]] are usually cited.<ref name="Ponter_2013"/> In 1960, {{Interlanguage link|Mikhail Mikhailovich Khrushchov|ru|Хрущов, Михаил Михайлович}} and Mikhail Alekseevich Babichev published a [[multiple discovery|similar model]] as well.<ref name="Khrushchov_1960"/> In modern literature, the relation is therefore also known as '''Reye–Archard–Khrushchov wear law'''. In 2022, the steady-state Archard wear equation was extended into the running-in regime using the [[Abbott-Firestone_curve|bearing ratio curve]] representing the initial [[surface topography]].<ref name="Varenberg_2022"/>

==Equation==
:<math>Q = \frac {KWL}H</math>
where:<ref name="Archard_1953"/>

: ''Q'' is the total volume of wear debris produced 
: ''K'' is a dimensionless  constant
: ''W'' is the total normal load
: ''L'' is the sliding distance
: ''H'' is the [[hardness]] of the softest contacting surfaces

Note that <math>WL</math> is proportional to the work done by the friction forces as described by Reye's hypothesis.

Also, K is obtained from experimental results and depends on several parameters. Among them are surface quality, [[chemical affinity]] between the material of two surfaces, surface hardness process, [[heat transfer]] between two surfaces and others.

==Derivation==
The equation can be derived by first examining the behavior of a single asperity.
:
The local load <math>\, \delta W </math>, supported by an asperity, assumed to have a circular cross-section with a radius <math>\, a </math>, is:<ref name="TLP"/>

:<math>\delta W = P \pi {a^2} \,\!</math>

where ''P'' is the yield pressure for the asperity, assumed to be deforming plastically. ''P'' will be close to the indentation [[hardness]], ''H'', of the asperity.

If the volume of wear debris, <math>\, \delta V </math>, for a particular asperity is a hemisphere sheared off from the asperity, it follows that:
: <math> \delta V = \frac 2 3 \pi a^3 </math>

This fragment is formed by the material having slid a distance 2''a''

Hence, <math>\, \delta Q </math>, the wear volume of material produced from this asperity per unit distance moved is:

:<math> \delta Q = \frac {\delta V} {2a} = \frac {\pi a^2} 3 \equiv \frac {\delta W} {3P} \approx \frac {\delta W} {3H}</math> making the approximation that <math>\,P \approx H</math>

However, not all asperities will have had material removed when sliding distance 2''a''. Therefore, the total wear debris produced per unit distance moved, <math>\, Q </math> will be lower than the ratio of ''W'' to ''3H''. This is accounted for by the addition of a dimensionless constant ''K'', which also incorporates the factor 3 above. These operations produce the Archard equation as given above. Archard interpreted ''K'' factor as a probability of forming wear debris from asperity encounters.<ref name="Archard_1956"/> Typically for 'mild' wear, ''K''&nbsp;≈&nbsp;10<sup>&minus;8</sup>, whereas for 'severe' wear, ''K''&nbsp;≈&nbsp;10<sup>&minus;2</sup>. Recently,<ref name="Aghababaei_2016"/> it has been shown that there exists a critical [[length scale]] that controls the wear debris formation at the asperity level. This length scale defines a critical junction size, where bigger junctions produce debris, while smaller ones deform plastically.
